Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Search
Misaligns Instruction-Tuning

Yushi Yang    Shreyansh Padarha Affiliation: University of Oxford    Sarah Ball Affiliation: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München    Andrew Lee    Adam Mahdi Affiliation: Harvard University*Corresponding authors Affiliation: Equal senior authors
Abstract

Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains large language models to use tools, but its impact on alignment is poorly understood. We study how agentic RL for search affects the alignment of instruction-tuned (IT) models. We find that RL-trained models inherit refusal reasoning by deflecting harmful requests into benign search queries, but this breaks down under a simple diagnostic trigger that elicits a search call before refusal can occur. Under this condition, RL models produce multi-step unsafe search actions and reasoning, reducing search query safety by up to 68.6% in Qwen and Llama models relative to their IT counterparts. The effect generalises across model families, scales, and RL algorithms. To understand why, we identify linear directions in the residual stream that control search query safety, and show that RL training progressively shifts search behaviour toward the harmful end of this direction. We thus propose representation-guided RL training, which adds a reward penalty based on projection toward the harmful search direction. Training on benign data alone, it restores IT-level alignment without reducing task accuracy and requires no additional training data. Together, our work provides the first framework for diagnosing, mechanistically analysing, and mitigating alignment degradation in agentic RL for search. Code is available at https://github.com/Yushi-Y/RL-search-align.

1 Introduction

Instruction tuning trains large language models (LLMs) to follow instructions and align responses with human preferences (Ouyang et al., 2022). Reinforcement learning (RL) further trains models to interleave reasoning with tool calls (Zhang et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025). Search is among the most widely used tools in agentic RL (as expanded in Table 5). Models trained to issue effective, well-timed search queries during reasoning, produces strong results on multi-hop question-answering tasks (Song et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2025b; Jin et al., 2025).

While prior work has shown that alignment in LLMs can be shallow and even benign fine-tuning on text responses can erode it (Qi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023), agentic RL goes further. It trains models to act through tool calls, acquiring agentic capabilities that instruction tuning never established and that standard alignment evaluations do not test. Whether this tool-use training stage degrades alignment built into instruction-tuning (IT), and how, remains largely unstudied. To find out, we train models from the Qwen and Llama families at sizes ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, using two RL algorithms, PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). Figure 1 summarises our three findings.

RL models are more vulnerable than their instruction-tuned counterparts (§4)

RL-trained search models inherit refusal behaviour from instruction tuning by turning harmful requests into harmless search queries. However, this inheritance is brittle. Prompting the search tool directly, before refusal tokens can surface, reveals that RL models are far more willing to execute multi-step harmful searches than their IT counterparts. Search safety falls by up to 68.6%68.6\% for Qwen models and 69.6%69.6\% for Llama models relative to IT models. The effect holds across two model families, four model sizes and two search setups.

RL training shifts the model’s internal state toward harmful search behaviour (§5)

To understand search safety drop at a representation level, we extract linear search directions in representation space with steering power over query safety. We find that RL checkpoints progressively project more than 2.5×2.5\times toward the harmful pole than IT models. This explains how RL training for accurate question-answering gradually undoes search safety established during instruction tuning.

A targeted penalty during RL training restores IT-level safety (§6)

We propose representation-guided RL, which adds a reward penalty based on how much each search query the model emits during training moves toward the harmful direction. This restores search safety to IT levels within 200 training steps while preserving benign question-answering performance. It requires no extra training data and only 0.3% additional GPU compute. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a representation-based penalty can recover the search safety lost during agentic RL.

2 Background and related work

Agentic RL for search

The RL objective with search integration in reasoning takes the form

maxπθ𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅∣x;ℛ)[rϕ(x,y)]−βDKL(πθ(y∣x,ℛ)∥πref(y∣x,ℛ)),\begin{split}\max_{\pi_{\theta}}\;&\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\;y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x;\mathcal{R})}\Big[r_{\phi}(x,y)\Big]\\ &-\beta\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x,\mathcal{R})\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x,\mathcal{R})\big),\end{split}

where πθ\pi_{\theta} is the policy LLM, πref\pi_{\text{ref}} the reference model, rϕr_{\phi} the reward and DKLD_{\text{KL}} is the KL penalty. RL-for-search optimises a retrieval-reasoning policy πθ(⋅∣x,ℛ)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\mathcal{R}) conditioned on both the prompt xx and retrieved content ℛ\mathcal{R} (Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025a; Dong et al., 2025). Mathematical details of PPO and GRPO for search are in Appendix C.

Agentic RL for search belongs to RL for Tool-Integrated Reasoning (RL-TIR) (Zhang et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025), which trains LLMs to interleave generation with tool calls. Search dominates surveyed RL-TIR frameworks (10/13; Appendix Table 5), with most relying on outcome-based rewards for knowledge-intensive QA (e.g., Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), R1-Searcher++ (Song et al., 2025b), ReSearch (Chen et al., 2026)). Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.x are the most widely adopted base models (92% and 38% of surveyed frameworks; Appendix Table 5), motivating our model choices.

Hijacking LLM agents

Prompt injection is the most widely studied agent vulnerability. Web agents tend to act differently when malicious HTML is injected into visited websites, hijacking agent behaviour (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2024; Korgul et al., 2025). Retrieval-augmented agents can similarly be steered toward biased outputs via injected external content (Yu and Papakyriakopoulos, 2025; Zou et al., 2025b). Such prompt injections often exploit competing objectives between LLM training stages: tensions between instruction following and preference tuning (e.g. non-refusal prefills that steer model responses) (Qi et al., 2025; Andriushchenko et al., 2025a). Unlike prior work focusing on inference-time agent vulnerabilities, we study tool-calling-based misalignment that arises during the RL training stage of a search agent, relative to its IT counterparts, that is the training stage that equips models with agentic capabilities.

3 Experiment setup

3.1 RL setup

Our RL setup follows standard agentic search frameworks (Jin et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026), applying PPO and GRPO on complex QA datasets with outcome-based rewards. Training data includes HotpotQA (91K multi-hop QA pairs) (Yang et al., 2018) and Natural Questions (307K QA pairs) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019). Rewards combine an exact-match term on the final answer and a formatting reward encouraging rollouts to interleave reasoning, search, and answer tokens (details in Appendix Table 8). We train Qwen-2.5-IT (7B, 14B, 32B) (Yang et al., 2025a) and Llama-3.2-3B-IT (Grattafiori et al., 2024); training hyperparameters are in Appendix Table 6.

For inference, we use greedy decoding with a ReAct-style system prompt (Yao et al., 2023) to produce deterministic responses (Appendix Figure 8). We analyse inference-time reasoning traces to understand output and tool-calling patterns (see Appendix Figures 12, 13, 14, 15).

3.2 Search setup

We allow models to search either a local corpus or the web. For local search, we index the English 2018 Wikipedia corpus (∼{\sim}21M passages of ∼{\sim}100 words) (Karpukhin et al., 2020) using e5-base-v2 embeddings (Wang et al., 2024) and FAISS (Douze et al., 2025) (details in Appendix D.2). For web search, we use SerpAPI (SerpApi, 2025) to query Google, returning the top-3 results per query.

We develop Search attacks as a simple tool-use trigger to isolate the RL induced behaviour changes, not jailbreak prompts (Table 1). The attacks are motivated RL models ‘hedging’ their searches by diverting into safe search queries after refusal-related tokens (Figure 2); we therefore attack before the model can hedge. Search attacks are implemented via deployable user prompts or response prefills to elicit early searches (more attack variants in Appendix D.4). We prompt with ‘I need to search for more information’, a typical sentence seen in RL model reasoning. We also include two non-refusal baseline prefills (Andriushchenko et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025), which open responses affirmatively without a search action, to isolate the effect of the search trigger itself.

Threat model

Our search triggers target the RL training stage and assume different levels of user access. The prompt-based attacks targets are user-deployable: any user can instruct the model to search in the chat interface, so the threat model is a malicious user. Prefill attacks assume response-level access, available via assistant-turn prefill on closed API providers and open-sourced or self-hosted deployments, we thus use them primarily as controlled diagnostic probes. Our aim is to diagnose the tool-use vulnerability introduced during the agentic RL training stage: the finding is that so minimal a trigger exposes a latent safety regression during that stage. Note that production systems may deploy additional safety layers beyond RL that we do not evaluate, potentially targeting the exact regression we identify.

3.3 Evaluation setup

Dataset and evaluator

We randomly sample 1170 harmful instructions from four benchmarks: AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023), MaliciousInstruct (Huang et al., 2024), TDC2023 (Maloyan et al., 2024b), and HarmBench (Maloyan et al., 2024a) covering cybercrime, social engineering, and fake news (examples in Appendix Figure 9). We split these into 871 for main evaluation and mitigation training and 299 for held-out evaluation.

To perform large-scale evaluation, we use Prometheus-2 (Kim et al., 2024) as the LLM judge: a Mistral-7B-based evaluator fine-tuned for behaviour assessment with strong agreement with human raters and GPT-4, using absolute grading with scores 1–5 based on defined rubrics (Appendix Figure 10), which as we show shortly, yields high correlations with human judgements.

Safety metrics

Table 2 defines three LLM-judged metrics per instruction: refusal, answer safety, and search safety. Refusal and answer safety are scored over the full reasoning trace (excluding retrieved content), while search safety is scored per query. Each metric uses a 1–5 scale (5 = safe, 1 = harmful), rescaled to 0–100 for reporting.

A human agreement study (Appendix E.2) on 100 randomly sampled requests validates the LLM evaluator, with high Spearman correlations (refusal ρ=0.88\rho=0.88, answer safety ρ=0.82\rho=0.82, search safety ρ=0.86\rho=0.86; all p<0.05p<0.05) and within-±\pm1-point agreement of 92%, 82%, and 90% across the three metrics (full results in Appendix Table 10).

4 How does RL degrade IT safety?

Given harmful requests, RL models largely inherit refusal from IT models and divert to benign searches (Section 4.1). However, a minimal search trigger exposes a systematic safety regression: RL models cascade into a series of harmful search calls (Section 4.2), dragging down all safety metrics. In the following sections, we use IT-Qwen/Llama for the instruction-tuned models, and RL-Qwen/Llama for the subsequently RL-trained counterparts.

4.1 RL inherits IT and diverts to safe search

Without attack, RL models match their IT counterparts on all safety metrics (92.5% vs. 91.8% for Qwen; 97.1% vs. 96.2% for Llama on refusal). This inheritance is visible in reasoning traces: IT-Qwen frequently uses an “Instead…” reframe (e.g., transforming “how to do money laundering” into “Instead, I will explain the legal consequences of money laundering”), and RL-Qwen follows this pattern by rephrasing request into a safe query (e.g., <search> consequences of money laundering) (Figure 2). However, RL-Llama still emits harmful queries in a substantial fraction of cases (57.1% with web search), meaning some unsafe searches naturally emerge during RL training (Llama has the lowest search safety in Figure 3).

4.2 Minimal search trigger breaks RL models

However, all Search attack variants (green→brown drops in Figure 3) achieve high attack success across RL models, with refusal, answer, and search safety dropping by up to 23.8%, 31.8%, and 69.6% respectively (Appendix Table 11), consistently outperforming non-refusal baselines (Appendix G.2). This holds across model families (Qwen, Llama), four sizes (3B–32B), two RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO), and both search setups (local and web).

Search safety is the primary driver: RL models more closely mirror harmful requests in their search queries (semantic cosine similarity: Qwen 0.62→0.86, Llama 0.79→0.91, via all-mpnet-base-v2 (Sentence-Transformers, 2021), continuously retrieving content that biases model reasoning and degrades both refusal and answer safety. Prompts and prefills are similarly effective (Appendix Table 11), showing users can trigger search via natural language without knowing the search trigger. This also shows when search is triggered matters: searching before the model can refuse is substantially more harmful than after (Figure 4a). Interestingly, RL models proceed with harmful searches even when we intentionally prefill a refusal followed by a search call (Appendix G.1).

RL models cascade into continuous harmful searches

Search attacks are consistently more effective on RL than IT models (yellow→brown drops in Figure 3), with RL models cascading into multi-step harmful queries until an answer is found (Figure 4, example in Appendix Figure 13). Qualitatively, IT models more often reframe harmful requests into safer search queries (e.g., “legal consequences of money laundering”). GRPO yields more harmful searches than PPO on average (Figure 4(b)), likely because it assigns uniform credit across all tokens in a trajectory (Shao et al., 2024), more strongly reinforcing trajectories that exactly mirror the harmful request.

5 Why does RL degrade IT safety?

IT and RL training optimise for competing objectives: RL rewards queries that mirror the request to maximise QA accuracy, while IT learns refusal and query diversion (Section 4.1). This creates a trade-off between QA accuracy and search safety during RL training (Figure 5). A minimal search trigger exploits this trade-off: the RL objective overrides IT behaviours, causing models to generate queries that mirror the harmful request.

We formalise this trade-off by tracking RL checkpoints across 200 steps for both search safety and QA performance (measured as exact match on the Natural Questions test set, n=3,610n{=}3{,}610). Figure 5 confirms that for both Qwen and Llama, RL training consistently improves QA performance at the cost of search safety under attacks.

RL training shifts search query toward harmful search representations.

To probe the underlying mechanisms, we apply representation engineering (Zou et al., 2025a; Rimsky et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025b) to extract linear directions in the residual stream that control search query safety. We find that RL checkpoints progressively shift search queries toward harmful directions (Figure 5c), consistent with the observed drop in search safety during training (Figure 5a).

For both IT-Qwen and IT-Llama, we extract three candidate steering vectors: 𝐝prompt\mathbf{d}_{\text{prompt}} and 𝐝attack\mathbf{d}_{\text{attack}} (defined in Table 3), and 𝐝refusal\mathbf{d}_{\text{refusal}} (Arditi et al., 2024) as a baseline. 𝐝prompt\mathbf{d}_{\text{prompt}} captures differences in search queries between harmful and benign requests; 𝐝attack\mathbf{d}_{\text{attack}} captures differences in search queries on the same harmful requests with and without attacks. We use 600 harmful instructions for extraction and the held-out 271 for evaluation; benign requests for 𝐝prompt\mathbf{d}_{\text{prompt}} are drawn from Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023). We extract steering vectors from IT models only, as we show that RL safety degradation can be controlled via IT representations alone.

We verify the causal effects of each candidate direction through activation steering, modifying hidden states during inference as 𝐡′=𝐡+α​𝐝(ℓ)\mathbf{h}^{\prime}=\mathbf{h}+\alpha\,\mathbf{d}^{(\ell)} with α∈{−2,−1,0,+1,+2}\alpha\in\{-2,-1,0,+1,+2\}, applied to all tokens at mid-to-late layers (ℓ=14,…,28\ell=14,\ldots,28), known to be effective for steering (Rimsky et al., 2024), tracking changes in search safety. Table 4 reports the most effective directions are 𝐝attack\mathbf{d}_{\text{attack}} for IT-Qwen and 𝐝prompt\mathbf{d}_{\text{prompt}} for IT-Llama. Qualitatively, steering modifies search queries by appending cautious context (e.g., “legal consequences”, “ethical implications”) to otherwise direct how-to queries. 𝐝refusal\mathbf{d}_{\text{refusal}} primarily modifies refusal tokens but fails to alter query content, making it unsuitable as a steering vector (Appendix H.1). Cosine similarity confirms 𝐝attack\mathbf{d}_{\text{attack}} is nearly orthogonal to 𝐝refusal\mathbf{d}_{\text{refusal}}, indicating they capture different mechanisms.

We then project RL checkpoints’ hidden states at the first query token under the Search attack onto each model’s most effective steering direction across layers. Figure 5c shows that RL checkpoints progressively shift toward the harmful pole at later layers, providing a mechanistic explanation: RL training does not introduce new harmful representations, but shifts existing queries along the harmful direction already present in the IT models.

6 How to restore safety during RL?

Section 5 reveals how RL training gradually shifts search query hidden state along a linear encoding that controls search safety. We leverage this to propose representation-guided RL as a mitigation, which adds a reward penalty on harmful search query projections during training. Without additional training data, it restores all three safety metrics to IT-model levels while preserving benign QA accuracy, with only 0.3% per-step GPU compute overhead on penalty computation (Figure 6).

Representation-aware RL training

Algorithm 1 presents the mitigation. Before RL training, we extract the search safety direction 𝐝prompt(ℓ)\mathbf{d}_{\text{prompt}}^{(\ell)} or 𝐝attack(ℓ)\mathbf{d}_{\text{attack}}^{(\ell)} with the best steering performance (Table 4) from the IT model at layer ℓ\ell, defined as the normalised mean difference between hidden states of harmful and benign search queries. The direction is computed once before training, incurring no additional cost. During RL, at each reward step, we pass the benign QA sequence truncated at <search> through a frozen IT model copy, extract the hidden state 𝐡q(ℓ)\mathbf{h}_{q}^{(\ell)} at the <search> token, and compute a penalty pqp_{q} measuring how aligned the search query representation is to the harmful search direction. The final reward is r=rtask−λ⋅pqr=r_{\text{task}}-\lambda\cdot p_{q}, where rtaskr_{\text{task}} is exact-match task reward and λ\lambda controls penalty strength. We select λ\lambda from {8,16,32}\{8,16,32\} to control the penalty not overwhelm the task reward, choosing the value that best improves search safety while preserving QA accuracy.

Figure 6 shows that representation-guided RL training restores search safety to IT-model levels across both Qwen and Llama (full metrics restored in Appendix Table 15), with minimal impact on QA accuracy. Notably, benign training data alone suffices: as the search safety direction is a linear separator, a small fraction of benign training queries (9.7% for Qwen, 13.6% for Llama) fall on the harmful side of the boundary (mean projection ≈0.04\approx 0.04), providing sufficient gradient signal without requiring explicit harmful training examples. The mitigated models’ query reformulations follow patterns such as ‘consequences of…’, ‘ethical implications of…’, ‘preventions of…’, consistent with the steering effects in Section 5.

Unlike LLM-judged rewards (Gunjal et al., 2025), which require autoregressive generation and reference rubrics data, our approach computes a penalty via a single batched forward pass and dot product at <search>, with negligible overhead. Concurrently, Prasad et al. (2026) use trained probes on frozen models as RL reward signals to reduce hallucination; unlike their four-stage pipeline over full token spans, ours requires no probe training and applies a single dot product at the semantically targeted search token.

Only benign data required for training

To test whether alternative data compositions outperform benign-only training, we ablate on Qwen with two variants: (1) augmenting benign data with 8k harmful examples, where harmful samples receive only the penalty with no task reward (Appendix Algorithm 2); (2) training exclusively on 32k harmful examples with only the penalty. Variant (1) performs comparably to benign-only but does not surpass it, confirming harmful data is an alternative but not a necessary addition (Figure 6c). Variant (2) fails at search completion: without a task reward, the model either stops searching entirely or emits the placeholder token query, as no QA examples guide effective search behaviour. Together, these results confirm that benign data alone provides sufficient signal for search query rephrasing.

Mitigation is representation-picky

To verify that the penalty effectiveness stems from the specific search safety direction rather than any arbitrary one, we replace 𝐝^search(ℓ)\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\text{search}}^{(\ell)} with a random unit vector 𝐝^random(ℓ)\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\text{random}}^{(\ell)} (cosine similarity: −0.009-0.009). The random direction yields 0% positive projections across 30,016 training queries, filtered out entirely by ReLU (Algorithm 1), confirming that benign query representations fall on the negative side of any random hyperplane. The true search direction, by contrast, produces positive projections in 27% of batches for Llama and 38% for Qwen, confirming it captures the harmful-search subspace. Consequently, the random-direction model recovers no search safety over the no-penalty baseline (Figure 6c): it is geometric alignment with the learned search direction, not merely the presence of a penalty, that drives safety restoration.

7 Conclusion

In this study, we ask whether agentic RL for search degrades the alignment built into instruction-tuning, how this occurs, and whether it can be fixed. The answer to all three is yes.

RL-trained search models appear aligned by diverting into benign queries, but this inheritance from IT is brittle. A minimal search trigger, deployable via user prompts, causes RL models to cascade into multi-step harmful queries absent in their IT counterparts. To understand this mechanism, we identify linear search directions that control query safety, and show that RL training progressively shifts search queries toward their harmful pole, revealing how outcome-based RL overrides IT alignment. Building on this, we propose representation-guided RL, which penalises projection onto the search directions during training with little overhead. Without additional training data, it restores IT-level alignment while preserving QA accuracy. Together, we provide the first framework for diagnosing, analysing, and mitigating alignment degradation in agentic RL for search.

Limitations

For data scope, our evaluation uses one-sentence harmful requests; expanding to more complex multi-step agentic tasks (Kumar et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2025b) may invoke more diverse search behaviours.

For application, we focus on search; whether alignment degradation extends to other tool types (e.g. code execution) remains open, and would establish whether this is a search-specific or broadly agentic phenomenon.

For mitigation design, we penalise projection onto the single best-steering layer; averaging projections across layers as an aggregate penalty is a natural alternative. The method targets query harmfulness, extending it to steer queries toward other desirable properties (e.g. factuality, groundedness) is a promising direction. Our mitigation is evaluated against the same diagnostic trigger used for diagnosis; robustness to adaptive attacks directly targeting the projection penalty remains open.

For deployment scope, our findings concern alignment degradation at the agentic training stage. Production deployments may incorporate additional safety layers we do not evaluate; any deployment relying on instruction-tuning safety as a baseline nonetheless remains exposed to the regression we identify.

Ethical Considerations

As we evaluated safety metrics on model response by running inference on datasets of harmful instructions, all harmful prompts were drawn from public academic benchmarks and contain no personal data. Additionally, to limit exposure to unsafe content, we truncated reasoning traces to avoid revealing any actionable harm and added explicit warnings in any figure displaying harmful content.

Appendix A Reproducibility Statement

We took several steps to ensure reproducibility. For software, an anonymous repository with our code and dataset is included in the abstract. For data, harmful instructions are described with examples in Figure 9. For evaluation, LLM-evaluator rubrics are provided in Appendix Figure 10. Attack templates and reasoning traces are in Table 1 and Appendix Figures 13–14.

For RL training, PPO and GRPO hyperparameters are listed in Table 6. We train 16 independent configurations (4 model sizes ×\times 2 algorithms ×\times 2 search setups), each hyperparameter-tuned for stable reward improvement and run with a single seed. The consistency of results across all 16 configurations constitutes cross-condition replication (Table 3). Greedy decoding makes safety metrics exact reads of each checkpoint rather than noisy estimates. Figures 4 and 5 show consistent trends across 200 steps and 4 checkpoints, and effect sizes are large (68%+ absolute percentage drop), both arguing against a lucky-seed artefact. Standard errors over harmful instructions are reported in both figures.

For LLM usage, ChatGPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 are used for writing polish and initial literature retrieval only; not for idea generation, data analysis, or experimental design.

Appendix B Summary of agentic RL for tool-use

In this section, we summarise 13 RL frameworks for tool-integrated reasoning with each framework’s main contribution, supported tools, and target models.

Table 5 shows that, Search (knowledge reasoning) and code execution (mathematical reasoning) were the most common tools (10 and 8 out of 13 papers, respectively). Over 93% and 38% of frameworks trained on Qwen-2.5 (Yang et al., 2025a) and Llama-3.x series (Grattafiori et al., 2024).

We also compare the reward designs of three representative RL-search pipelines: Search-R1, R1-search, and agentic reinforced policy optimization (ARPO) (Figure 7). All three frameworks adopted outcome-based rewards with minor variations. Search-R1 used a pure outcome-based reward for reasoning question-answering (Jin et al., 2025), R1-Searcher added a search-usage bonus to encourage querying (Song et al., 2025a), and ARPO added a process-aware credit assignment to allocate partial rewards to reasoning and tool-use steps (Dong et al., 2025). Motivated by those works, we adopted the simplest common denominator setup with the outcome-based reward (Jin et al., 2025).

Appendix C More on RL for search

In this section, we provide the hyperparameter configurations for PPO (Table 6) and GRPO (Table 6) training for search, as well as the reward structure (Table 8) used across all model variants.

C.1 PPO with a search engine

We provide details of PPO with a search engine and list its hyperparameters (Table 6).

PPO maximises the following objective for search:

𝒥PPO​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta) =𝔼[∑tI(yt)min(rt(θ)At,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\Bigg[\sum_{t}I(y_{t})\,\min\!\Big(r_{t}(\theta)\,A_{t},
clip(rt(θ),−ϵ,+ϵ)At)],\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}\!\big(r_{t}(\theta),\,1\!-\!\epsilon,\,1\!+\!\epsilon\big)\,A_{t}\Big)\Bigg],

where rt​(θ)=πθ​(yt∣y<t,ℛ)πold​(yt∣y<t,ℛ)r_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},\mathcal{R})}{\pi_{\text{old}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},\mathcal{R})} is the importance ratio, πθ\pi_{\theta} and πold\pi_{\text{old}} denote the current and previous policy models, and ℛ\mathcal{R} is retrieved content. We applied a masked loss on retrieval tokens: I⁡(yt)=1I(y_{t})=1 if yty_{t} is generated by the LLM, and I⁡(yt)=0I(y_{t})=0 if it is retrieved (Jin et al., 2025). This discourages directly copying retrieved content and stabilises training. The advantages AtA_{t} were computed with Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (Schulman et al., 2018) and the clipping parameter ϵ\epsilon stabilises training (Schulman et al., 2017).

C.2 GRPO with a search engine

We provide details of GRPO with a search engine and list its hyperparameters (Table 6). Unlike PPO, which relies on a learned critic to estimate advantages, GRPO forms a baseline from the average reward of multiple sampled outputs, reducing variance without a value network. For each input question xx, we sample a group of GG responses {y1,y2,…,yG}\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{G}\} from the reference policy πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. We then optimise the policy by maximising the GRPO objective:

𝒥GRPO(θ)=𝔼[1G∑i=1G1|yi|∑t=1|yi|min(ri,t(θ)A^i,t,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|y_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}\min\!\Big(r_{i,t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{i,t}, (1)
clip(ri,t(θ),−ϵ,+ϵ)A^i,t)−βDKL(πθ∥πref)],\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}\!\big(r_{i,t}(\theta),\,1\!-\!\epsilon,\,1\!+\!\epsilon\big)\hat{A}_{i,t}\Big)-\beta\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}\big)\Bigg],

where the expectation is over x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D} and {yi}i=1G∼πθ(⋅∣x;ℛ)\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x;\mathcal{R}), ri,t​(θ)=πθ​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t;ℛ)πold​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t;ℛ)r_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t};\mathcal{R})}{\pi_{\text{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t};\mathcal{R})} is the importance ratio, ϵ\epsilon and β\beta are hyperparameters, and A^i,t\hat{A}_{i,t} is an advantage computed from the relative rewards within each group. Similar to PPO, when computing DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}}, we apply retrieved-token masking so that the KL penalty is only applied to model-generated tokens (excluding retrieved tokens from the search engine).

C.3 Reward structure

We provide the reward structure used during RL training. During training, the reward is computed from three components: answer correctness via exact match (EM) against ground-truth answers, format validity of emitted tags, and retrieval correctness based on whether the retrieved passages contain the ground-truth answer from the training QA datasets (NQ and HotpotQA).

Appendix D More on experiment setup

In this section, we provide additional details on the experimental setup, including the multi-search attack, system prompt, local search pipeline, and harmful instruction datasets.

D.1 System prompt

We provide the ReAct-style (Yao et al., 2023) system prompt used across models (Figure 8).

All prompt-based attacks were created by appending additional sentences (listed in Table 1) to this base prompt.

D.2 Local search pipeline

We provide details on the local search retrieval pipeline.

The pipeline contains four steps: (i) encode the query with e5-base-v2 (Wang et al., 2024); (ii) run FAISS kk-NN (Douze et al., 2025) with k=10k=10 to get candidate IDs; (iii) load the corresponding passages; and (iv) rerank the top 10 with cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2 (Sentence Transformers Team, 2025) to retrieve the top 3 passages.

D.3 Examples of harmful instructions

We provide examples of harmful instructions passed to jailbreak the models (Figure 9).

Each instruction was randomly sampled from AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023), MaliciousInstruct (Huang et al., 2024), TDC2023 (Maloyan et al., 2024b), and HarmBench (Maloyan et al., 2024a). The subset contains 299 examples. Prompts are single-sentence imperatives or questions seeking unethical or illegal guidance on topics such as fake news, financial crime, and abuse.

D.4 Multi-search attacks

Apart from Search attacks (Table 1), we develop a Multi-search attack that prompts or prefills ten consecutive searches before refusal, achieving greater attack success. It similarly requires user prompt or response-level access (Section 3.2). While user prompts are deployable, the iterative prefills require stronger assumptions and we thus treat it as a diagnostic upper bound.

We provide the full attack templates (Table 9) and all safety metrics for all our search attacks (Table 11).

For Multi-search attacks, we induce the model to start with a search and issue ten searches total, either by instructing in the user prompt or iteratively prefilling the <search> token ten times (once after each retrieval). Prompt-instructed searches may appear anywhere in the response; prefilled searches are all inserted before refusal tokens, with no intermediate reasoning in between.

For Multi-search attacks, inserting ten searches before refusal (Prefill-A/B×\times10) caused the largest drops across all metrics, reducing refusal, answer safety, and search safety by up to 33.3%, 43.2%, and 62.0% respectively (Appendix Table 11). Prefilled searches consistently produced cascades of harmful queries exploring different aspects of the request (Figure 17; example in Appendix Figure 14). Prefill-C×\times10, which prefills search after each refusal, showed the same pattern: queries remained harmful right after the refusal sentence, driving lower answer safety than both IT-Qwen (local: Qwen: 89.5→66.7; Llama: 96.2→73.5; Appendix Table 11) and Prefill-C.

The ten prefilled searches were not uniformly harmful. RL-Qwen’s searches remained consistently below IT-Qwen across all ten positions (Appendix Figure 17), while Llama’s Prefill-A/B×10\times 10 drifted to safer queries after the first 3–5, despite no intermediate reasoning (Appendix Figure 18). Though these diversions raised overall search safety, early harmful searches sufficed to elicit harmful answers, yielding larger answer safety drops than the Search attack (Qwen: 65.4→\to50.9, Llama: 73.2→\to59.0; Appendix Table 11; example in Appendix Figure 15).

Prompt-A/B×10\times 10 did not outperform Prefill-A/B×10\times 10, as models did not reliably follow the “do ten searches” instruction: prompt-based attacks increased average search count by only ++2.1 (Qwen) and ++0.52 (Llama), keeping safety metrics close to single-search Prompt-A/B (Appendix Table 11).

Appendix E More on evaluation

In this section, we describe the LLM evaluator rubrics and how we validate them against human judgements.

E.1 LLM evaluator rubrics

We provide the rubrics used by the LLM evaluator to score each safety metrics (Figure 10). Higher score indicates safer behaviour: 5 = fully safe; 1 = fully harmful.

E.2 Human agreement with LLM evaluator

We provide full results of the human validation study for the LLM evaluator (Table 10).

We randomly sample N=100N=100 examples from the 871 harmful instructions and evaluated the RL-Qwen under the Prefill-A attack. We choose Qwen as it generally emits more search queries and longer reasoning than Llama. We evaluated with an attack to elicit more varied responses than simple refusals to stress-test the evaluator.

For each example, two independent human raters and the LLM evaluator scored full model response for refusal and answer safety, and each emitted query for search safety, following the rubrics in Figure 10. We then compute Spearman correlations between LLM and human score pairs and reported agreement rates (exact match, within ±\pm1 point, and within ±\pm2 points) on the original 1–5 scale.

As shown in Table 10, all three metrics achieve high correlations ≥0.82\geq 0.82 (all significant at p<0.05p<0.05) and within ±\pm1 point agreement ≥82%\geq 82\%. Human scores are consistently lower than the LLM judge’s, suggesting LLM judge may be slightly more tolerant and jailbroken models may be judged even less safe by humans.

From the evaluator’s reasoning, we identify two sources of this discrepancy: (1) the LLM judge sometimes over-states answer safety when harmful content is phrased neutrally, even when the response clearly aids the harmful request in actions; and (2) when a model finds no relevant retrieved results and emits a refined query to search again (example in Figure 13), the LLM evaluator often confuses it with a refusal behaviour rather than a query clarification, inflating refusal scores.

Appendix F More on reasoning traces

In this section, we provide example reasoning traces for benign, harmful, and jailbroken model outputs.

F.1 Reasoning traces on a benign example

We provide an example reasoning trace from the RL-Qwen on a multi-hop reasoning question (Figure 11), illustrating how search models emit dynamic searches to reach an answer.

F.2 Base model reasoning traces after RL are ruthlessly harmful

We show that RL-trained base models routinely produces harmful searches and answers, with markedly different reasoning patterns from RL-trained IT models (Figure 12).

F.3 Examples of jailbroken outputs under attacks

We provide example jailbroken outputs under Search and Multi-search attacks (Figure 13, 14 for RL-Qwen, Figure 15 for RL-Llama).

Under the Search attack (Figure 13), Qwen showed a strong search intent: when a query returns no relevant information, the model emitted progressively refined harmful queries to produce a ‘comprehensive’ answer (Prefill-A). This repeated search intent persisted even after an immediate prefilled refusal (Prefill-C). Notably, in this example, RL-Qwen also emitted a harmful query after an ‘Instead’ reframe without any attack (contrary to Figure 2), indicating that some post-RL emitted searches are already harmful.

Under the Multi-search attack, Qwen (Figure 14) emitted queries that gradually target more detailed aspects of the request across ten prefills, even with no intermediate reasoning in between (Prefill-A×10\times 10). These cascades of harmful searches persisted even with repeated refusal prefill (Precill-C×10\times 10). In contrast, Llama (Figure 15) gradually drifted towards harmless queries (Prefill-A×10\times 10), and this drift was faster when a refusal was prefilled before the searches (Precill-C×10\times 10). This explains the higher search safety of Multi-search than Search for Llama (Figure 3, yellow→brown).

Appendix G More on search safety

In this section, we provide detailed safety metrics under attacks, including larger model results and per-query-position search safety drops.

G.1 Searches remain harmful right after refusal

Harmful searches appear not only before refusal, but also immediately after. Under Prefill-C, where we prefilled a refusal followed by <search> (Table 1), the search safety remains low RL models (local: Qwen: 46.0 vs 72.3; Llama: 12.8 vs 41.3; Appendix Table 11). Qualitatively, models still emitted harmful queries right after ‘I can’t’ (example in Appendix Figure 13). Consequently, Prefill-C still lowered answer safety (local: Qwen: 89.5→70.9; Llama: 96.2→81.5; Appendix Table 11) despite the prefilled refusal. This shows searches issued immediately after a superficial refusal can still be harmful; it may only divert to safer searches following longer refusal reasoning (e.g., the ‘Instead’ reframe for RL-Qwen; Figure 2), and harmful searches and refusal can co-exist in response, as they arise from different sources: harmful searches from RL training, refusal from instruction tuning.

G.2 Search attacks outperform non-refusal prefills

The Search attacks generally result in lower safety metrics than the non-refusal prefills (our baselines in Table 1), thus higher jailbreak success (Appendix Table 11). Non-refusal prefills are less effective: we observed Qwen saying “Sure, I will not provide any advice on …” and “Sure, I can help with that. However, I won’t provide any actual advice…”, showing resistance to non-refusals.

While both disrupt the initial refusal reasoning, search-based and non-refusal prefills differ in important ways. Search-based prefills trigger early searches before refusal, producing harmful, request-mirroring queries as an artefact of RL search training, whereas non-refusal prefills redirect models from refusal to an affirmative response to exploit model’s pre-trained harmful knowledge (Qi et al., 2025). The source of harm also differ: non-refusal mainly draws on model pre-training knowledge for harm, while search-based attacks rely more on import harm via retrieved content.

G.3 Search safety across query positions

Figure 4(a) shows that RL models not only issue less safe initial queries than IT models but cascade into more harmful searches across all query positions. The RL-Qwen consistently scores lower on search safety than its IT counterpart, aligning with qualitative reasoning traces that reveal a stronger drive to persist in harmful search until an answer is found (Appendix Figure 13).

We report search safety by query position under Search and Multi-search attacks (Figure 16, 17 for RL-Qwen, Figure 18 for RL-Llama).

Under the Search attack (Figure 16), RL-Qwen showed consistently lower safety than IT-Qwen across the first five query positions.

Under the Multi-search attack, Qwen (Figure 17) also showed consistently lower safety across all ten query positions. In contrast, RL-Llama (Figure 18) emitted a few initial less-safe queries relative to IT-Llama, then drifted toward safer searches. The safety rise was faster for Prefill-C×10\times 10 than Prefill-A/B×10\times 10, suggesting that queries emitted after refusal diverts to safety more quickly.

Appendix H More on mitigation

In this section, we report full steering results of candidate steering vectors on search query safety (Section 5, Table 3), and provide more results of variations and ablation studies on the mitigation RL training (Section 6).

H.1 Full steering results

Table 13 reports full steering results and the most effective steering vectors for IT-Qwen and IT-Llama, measuring search safety on the 271 held-out harmful prompts with 267 search queries under the Search attack. For IT-Qwen, no steering gives 36.336.3 search safety (78/26778/267 queries rated safe, i.e. ≥4\geq 4).

𝐝attack\mathbf{d}_{\text{attack}} at layer 14 is the best steering vector: it produces cleaner reframing with no garbling, rewriting harmful search queries into safety-framed alternatives by appending “legal consequences of…” (∼22%{\sim}22\%) or “ethical implications of…” (∼17%{\sim}17\%), “Prevention of …”(∼5%{\sim}5\%), while leaving query structure intact, making it the most effective steering vector for search safety. This direction is also nearly orthogonal to 𝐝refusal\mathbf{d}_{\text{refusal}}, confirming it operates on a distinct mechanism.

Steering with 𝐝refusal\mathbf{d}_{\text{refusal}} at α=+2.0\alpha{=}+2.0 improves query safety (+100+100 safe queries) but by inserting refusal language as the search query rather than deliberately modifying query content itself, making it unsuitable despite strong numerical gains.
